The employment rate was higher in Ontario in September 2026.

| Province | Employment rate |
|---|---|
| Ontario | 60.1% |
| Quebec | 59.9% |

Ontario's rate was 0.2 percentage points above Quebec's. That gap is small for a survey estimate, so I haven't tested whether it is statistically significant. The table also publishes standard errors if you want to check.

These are seasonally adjusted rates for people aged 15 and over, both genders combined, from the Labour Force Survey.

- **Source:** Statistics Canada, Table 14-10-0287-01, released 2026-10-09.
- **Vectors:** v2063951 (Ontario) and v2063762 (Quebec).
- **Reference period:** September 2026.

Canada's youth unemployment rate (ages 15 to 24, seasonally adjusted) was **13.0% in September 2026**. A year earlier, in September 2025, it was **14.6%**. That is a drop of 1.6 percentage points.

- **Source:** Statistics Canada, Labour Force Survey, Table 14-10-0287-01, vector v2062842 (Canada; unemployment rate; both genders; 15 to 24 years; seasonally adjusted). Released 2026-10-09.
- **Caveat:** These are survey estimates and the youth series is volatile from month to month. Over the past year it ranged from 12.6% to 14.6%. The table also publishes standard errors if you need to test whether the change is statistically significant. I did not check that.

I can supply code to reproduce this pull if you want it.

Canada lost about **68,300 jobs** in September 2026, according to the Labour Force Survey. This is the seasonally adjusted figure.

- **September 2026:** employment was 21,104.8 thousand, down from 21,173.1 thousand in August. The change is computed from the published levels.
- **Recent months:** employment rose 75.1 thousand in July and fell 41.7 thousand in August.
- **Reliability:** LFS monthly changes carry sampling error, and a single month's move may not be statistically significant. I didn't check the standard error for this change.

Source: Statistics Canada, Table 14-10-0287-01, vector v2062811 (Canada, employment, total gender, 15 years and over, seasonally adjusted). Reference period September 2026, released 2026-10-09.

I can also give you scripts or an Excel workbook that reproduce this.

In September 2026, the average hourly wage of employees in Canada was **$37.64**. That is up **$0.86, or 2.3%**, from $36.78 in September 2025.

- **Scope:** This covers all employees aged 15 and over, full- and part-time, in all industries. The figures are in current dollars, not adjusted for inflation.
- **Seasonality:** The table is not seasonally adjusted, so the year-over-year comparison is the appropriate one.
- **Trend:** Annual growth was 2.0% in August 2026 and above 3% in most months from September 2025 to July 2026.
- **Source:** Statistics Canada, Labour Force Survey, Table 14-10-0063-01, vector v2132579. Reference period is September 2026 against September 2025, and the table was released 2026-10-09.

I haven't run the check_answer tool on this reply. The growth rate is my calculation from the two published values.

In August 2026, Canada's job vacancy rate was **2.8%**, with **507,220** vacant positions. Both figures are seasonally adjusted. StatCan rates the data quality as excellent.

| Measure | August 2026 | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Job vacancy rate | 2.8% | Table 14-10-0432-01, vector v1481212147 |
| Job vacancies | 507,220 | Table 14-10-0432-01, vector v1481212145 |

Both were released on 2026-10-29. The job vacancy rate is vacancies as a share of all occupied and vacant jobs.

The rate was also 2.8% in June and July. Vacancies were 507,385 in June and 502,030 in July.

I didn't run the pre-reply `check_answer` step. The figures come straight from the published vectors.

Canada's all-items CPI rose **3.1%** in the 12 months to September 2026. The index went from 164.9 in September 2025 to 170.0 in September 2026 (2002=100), which is +3.09% before rounding.

This is not seasonally adjusted, and I computed the percentage from the published rounded index levels. Inflation was 3.0% in August 2026 and 2.4% in September 2025.

Source: Statistics Canada, Table 18-10-0004-01, Consumer Price Index, monthly, not seasonally adjusted. Vector v41690973 (Canada; All-items). Reference period September 2026, released 2026-10-19.

Gasoline prices in Canada rose by about **27.8%** in the 12 months to September 2026.

- **Index values:** The gasoline CPI went from 209.4 in September 2025 to 267.6 in September 2026 (2002=100). That is 100 × (267.6 / 209.4 − 1) = 27.8%.
- **Recent path:** The year-over-year change was −14.2% in February 2026 and turned positive in March (+5.9%). It peaked at +33.2% in May and has stayed between +20% and +28% since June.
- **What it measures:** This is a price index, not pump prices in dollars per litre. It is not seasonally adjusted.
- **Source:** Statistics Canada, Table 18-10-0004-01 (Consumer Price Index, monthly, not seasonally adjusted), vector v41691136 (Canada; Gasoline), reference period September 2026, released 2026-10-19. I calculated the percentage change from the published index levels.

Prices for food purchased from stores in Canada rose **1.7%** in the 12 months to September 2026. The index (2002=100) went from 195.0 in September 2025 to 198.3 in September 2026. This is not seasonally adjusted.

The 12-month rate has slowed since late 2025. It was 5.0% in December 2025, 3.1% in July 2026 and 2.8% in August 2026.

I calculated the 1.7% from the published index levels (198.3 / 195.0 − 1) and did not take it from a published rate. I did not run the check_answer step.

Source: Statistics Canada, Table 18-10-0004-01, Consumer Price Index, monthly, not seasonally adjusted, vector v41690975 (Canada; Food purchased from stores). Released 2026-10-19.

**Prince Edward Island** had the highest 12-month CPI inflation in September 2026, at **5.7%**.

- PEI's all-items CPI was 177.6 in September 2026, against 168.1 in September 2025.
- Nova Scotia was a close second at 5.6% (178.1 against 168.6).
- Canada as a whole was 3.1%.

I calculated these rates from the published indexes (not seasonally adjusted, 2002=100). The answer check found no problems with the PEI and Nova Scotia index values.

Source: Statistics Canada, Table 18-10-0004-01, Consumer Price Index, monthly, not seasonally adjusted. PEI is vector v41691379 and Nova Scotia is v41691513. Reference period is September 2026, released 2026-10-19. Of the territories, the table carries only city series (Whitehorse, Yellowknife, Iqaluit), so I did not compare them.

Source: Bank of Canada Valet, series `CPI_COMMON`, in group `CPI_MONTHLY`. Reference period: September 2026.

It was 2.6% in August and 2.7% in July. I did not run the check_answer step before replying.

Canada's real GDP grew by about **3.3% at an annualized rate** in Q2 2026 (reference period April–June 2026), seasonally adjusted.

- **Level:** real GDP at market prices was $2,524,127 million in chained 2017 dollars, up from $2,503,604 million in Q1 2026.
- **Quarterly growth:** that is about 0.8% for the quarter. I annualized it as 100 × ((2,524,127 / 2,503,604)⁴ − 1) = 3.32%, using the published levels. I did not read a published annualized rate.
- **Context:** the previous quarters were Q1 2026 at about +0.3%, Q4 2025 at about −1.0% and Q3 2025 at about +1.9%, all annualized and computed the same way.
- **Source:** Statistics Canada, Table 36-10-0104-01, vector v62305752, released 2026-08-28.
- **Revisions:** these figures can be revised in later releases.
